title: Ajrakh
descriptionHtml:
Ajrakh is a traditional form of hand block printing and resist dyeing that uses natural  colours such as indigo, madder and printed mordants. The word Ajrakh has two meanings: "keep it for today" and "like the blue sky with stars sparkling in the darkness". The textiles are treated with vegetable and mineral colors and the fabric goes through a washing cycle about eight times. Wooden and metal blocks carved with traditional designs are coated in dye and printed on cloth. The resulting fabric is known for its rich and bold colors.

Ajrakh is primarily found in Sindh, Pakistan, and the village of Ajrakhpur in the bordering Kutch district of India. Other places that produce Ajrakh include Barmer in Rajasthan, India

title: Applique
descriptionHtml: Appliqué is a decorative textile technique where fabric pieces are cut into shapes and artfully stitched onto a larger base fabric to create intricate designs and patterns. Often enhanced with embroidery, beads, or mirrors, appliqué transforms plain cloth into vibrant works of art. From the bold, colorful motifs of Odisha’s famous Pipli appliqué to the delicate detailing seen in global quilting traditions, this craft beautifully blends creativity with skill. It is widely used in garments, home décor, and ceremonial textiles, making it both an artistic and cultural expression of storytelling through fabric.

title: Baluchari & Swarnachari
descriptionHtml:
Baluchari sarees, originating from Bishnupur, or Bankura in West Bengal, are masterpieces of storytelling woven into silk. Known for their rich texture and intricate pallus, these sarees are adorned with motifs inspired by epics like the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and tales from Indian mythology.  

Swarnachari sarees are a regal variant of the Baluchari, woven in the same tradition but elevated with the opulence of zari. Their borders and pallus often showcase mythological tales, floral vines, and temple-inspired designs, but with a luminous shimmer that adds richness. Known as the "queen of silks" from Bengal, Swarnachari sarees are coveted bridal and festive drapes, blending storytelling artistry with royal elegance.

title: Banarasi / Benarasi!
descriptionHtml: Unveiling the timeless elegance of Banarasi (pronounced Be-naa-ra-see) sarees! Originating from the ancient city of Benaras (modern day Varanasi), these exquisite wonders are crafted with intricate designs and rich brocade work. Often featuring silk and shimmering Zari, they feature a variety of motifs like the Teercha body, the Kaduwa border, the Tilfi and the Alfi buttis. The sheer craftsmanship and luxurious feel make them a true heirloom. New age Benarasis are also part of this collection, including delicate varieties- georgette and the ever-popular kora sarees!

title: Bandhej Bandhani
descriptionHtml: Bandhani sarees originate from the colorful state of Gujarat and are a testament to meticulous craftsmanship. This intricate tie-and-dye technique involves meticulously tying the fabric into little dots on patterns (bandh means tie in Gujarati), creating a mesmerizing play of geometric patterns. Skilled artisans use natural dyes and resist-dyeing methods to achieve vibrant colors and intricate designs. Shop beautiful chunri lehengas, sarees, suit fabrics in bandhani on Silkenthread.

title: Batik
descriptionHtml: Batik sarees, captivating works of art on fabric, originate from Indonesia. This ancient technique involves applying wax resist patterns onto the fabric. The uncovered areas are then dyed, creating vibrant colors and beautiful, flowy designs. Once the wax is removed, the final masterpiece is revealed. Each Batik saree is unique, as the hand-waxing process introduces subtle variations. Silken Thread brings you a curated collection of Batik sarees, where age-old artistry meets modern elegance.

descriptionHtml: A collection of block prints from different parts of India. With Kalamkari featuring completely filled in coloured blocks, Bagh prints featuring detailed floral and fauna (in larger blocks) and Bagru its characteristic small repeated iconography, they create a rich fabric, taking into account local colours and themes. Of course, modern block printing artisans frequently combine these styles to create new, gorgeous patterns filled with a range of motifs and colours derived from new age materials. title: Dhakai-Jamdani
descriptionHtml:
Jamdani was originally known as Dhakai (Daccai)... named after the city of Dhaka (Dacca), one of many ancient textile weaving centers in Bengal region. Under the Mughal Empire the Persian term Jamdani came to be in popular use, since it was the court language of the Mughals.

Dhakai Jamdani is known for its delicate texture, unique design, and thread work. Unlike printed fabrics, these lightweight wonders boast motifs meticulously woven directly into the fabric using a unique weft technique. The sarees are usually made of lightweight, translucent cotton that hugs the body and features handcrafted floral motifs. UNESCO has declared the art of weaving Dhakai Jamdani to be an "Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity". Discover the artistry of Jamdani at Silken Thread.

title: Dhaniakhali Sarees
descriptionHtml:
Dhaniakhali cotton sarees originate from Dhaniakhali, a historic weaving centre in West Bengal known for its strong yet breathable cotton textiles. Traditionally woven in natural off-white or earthy tones, these sarees are distinguished by bold, contrasting borders and characteristic stripes or checks on the pallu. The cotton used is crisp and durable, making Dhonekhali sarees especially suited to India’s warm climate while retaining a dignified, structured drape that reflects everyday elegance.

What sets Dhonekhali cotton sarees apart is their quiet versatility and deep cultural roots. Often adorned with simple temple motifs or geometric patterns, they balance functionality with aesthetic restraint. Worn widely for daily use, office wear, and religious occasions, these sarees represent the essence of Bengal’s handloom tradition—unpretentious, sustainable, and timeless. Over the years, contemporary colour palettes and design updates have helped Dhonekhali cottons stay relevant while preserving the integrity of the original craft.

title: Gota Patti work
descriptionHtml:
Gotta Patti work, also known as “Lappe ka kaam or gota kinari work,” is one of the most famous and among the art craft gems of India. Gota Patti is a unique embellishment to enhance the fabric look, making it rich and splendid for occasion or wedding wear.

Gota patti is mainly used on lightweight fabrics like chiffon, georgette, tussar silks and crepes. The different forms of gota patti include seekhi(lace trim), phool(circles resembling flowers), bijiya(triangular lace trim), bakhandi and lappa(applique), among others.

Gotta Patti sarees have their roots in the royal courts of Rajasthan, India. These sarees are known for their opulent look and luxurious feel, making them perfect for wedding saree.  These borders come alive with shimmering embellishments like beads, sequins, and tiny mirrors. title: Kalamkari
descriptionHtml:
Kalamkari (literally translated to art made with a Qalam or a pen) is an art that originated in the modern day states of Andhra pradesh and Telangana several hundred years ago. It involves multiple steps to prepare the fabric for painting and uses only natural dyes. The colors used in Kalamkari are earthy tones of reds, blues, greens, yellows, and browns. Women are depicted in shades of yellow, gods in blue, and demons in red and green.

There are two identifiable types of Kalamkari: Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam. In Machilipatnam(Peddana) style, Kalamkari designs are generally printed with hand carved blocks with intricate details. The Srikalahasti style includes Kalamkari designs inspired from Hindu mythology, that describe the scenes from the epics.

title: Kanjeevaram
descriptionHtml: The Kanjeevaram saree, originating from the town of Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu, India, is renowned for its exquisite craftsmanship and luxurious silk fabric. Known for intricate designs, and use of real gold zari for an unparalleled luxe look. Each Kanjeevaram silk saree is a true heirloom, the craft passed down through generations of weavers, ensuring you get a piece of India's cultural heritage. Silken Thread brings the opulence of pure Kanjeevaram sarees directly to you. Explore our online collection and discover the beauty and the grace of these weaves.

title: Kantha
descriptionHtml:
Kantha, also spelled kanta or qanta, is a type of embroidery craft in Bangladesh and eastern regions of India, particularly in the Indian states of West Bengal, Tripura and Odisha. This running stitch is associated with rural weaving and has liberated many rural weavers in ever evolving Bengal. 

Modern day Kantha is a combination of the running stitch for outlines and 'bhorat' stitches used as filler. The designs of Kantha saree are taken from day-to-day life, depicting folk stories , epics, mythological background, geometric designs, ritualistic motifs, luxurious vegetation with roaming animals, running dear, dancing peacock, temples etc. “Kalka” is an important motif, (a cone or mango shaped,) embroidered in association with spiral whirls, broad band of circles, lotus or heart shaped foliage.

Explore Silken Thread's collection and discover the soul of storytelling beautifully expressed in fabric.

title: Kasavu
descriptionHtml: Kasavu weave is a distinctive handwoven textile tradition from Kerala, celebrated for its understated elegance and cultural significance. Traditionally woven from fine, unbleached cotton, the fabric is characterized by its plain ivory body contrasted with shimmering borders made using gold or silver-toned zari, known as kasavu. The beauty of the weave lies in its simplicity, where clean lines, balanced proportions, and meticulous craftsmanship create a fabric that is both graceful and timeless. Woven on handlooms by skilled artisans, Kasavu textiles require precision to seamlessly integrate the lustrous border into the lightweight cotton base. Deeply associated with festivals, weddings, temple rituals, and the harvest festival of Onam, Kasavu has become a symbol of Kerala's heritage, purity, and refined aesthetic. While contemporary interpretations introduce colored borders, motifs, and innovative designs, the essence of the Kasavu weave remains rooted in its minimalist elegance and centuries-old weaving traditions.

title: Madhubani
descriptionHtml: Madhubani, also known as Mithila art, is a centuries-old folk painting tradition that blossomed in the Mithila region of Bihar. Characterised by bold lines, intricate patterns, and vibrant natural colours, Madhubani art narrates stories of mythology, nature, and village life. Artists typically use twigs, matchsticks, or even fingers to create the rhythmic geometric motifs that define the style. Traditionally drawn on mud walls during festivals and auspicious occasions, the art form has evolved beautifully onto textiles, paper, and contemporary decor. Every Madhubani piece carries a distinct handmade charm—celebrating heritage, symbolism, and the timeless creativity of rural artisans.

title: Paithanis
descriptionHtml: Crafted meticulously from the finest silk, Paithani sarees are adorned with intricate motifs inspired by nature, folklore, and royal symbols, reflecting the opulence of bygone eras. Originating in the town of Paithan, Maharashtra, this exquisite drape boasts a rich history dating back over 2000 years. Muniya Paithani, a unique variety, features intricate geometric patterns, while the original Paithani saree showcases intricate motifs inspired by nature and ancient art. Woven from the finest silk and adorned with pure Zari, original handloom Paithani sarees are renowned for their exceptional quality and specialty in double-sided weaving, making them identical on both sides, as compared to powerloom sarees, where the back of the saree has miscellaneous threads from the zari weaving.

title: Parsi
descriptionHtml: Parsi embroideries have their origins in the Parsi community of India. Parsi sarees, a testament to the rich heritage of the Parsi community, boast intricate needlework and vibrant colors. The 'gara' technique, the heart of Parsi embroidery, involves using silk floss to create delicate floral or geometric designs. These sarees often depict Zoroastrian motifs, reflecting the community's unique cultural identity.

title: Patolas

title: Phulkari
descriptionHtml:
Phulkari is a traditional Punjabi embroidery technique that uses colorful silk thread and a darn stitch to create geometric and floral patterns on coarse cotton fabricThe word "phulkari" translates to "flower work" in Hindi and Punjabi, but the designs can also include cover motifs and other shapes. Phulkari is a hereditary craft that was traditionally practiced by women in the Punjab region, which is now part of both India and Pakistan.

Phulkari is known for its neat, regular patterns, and smaller stitches result in finer, better work. The base cloth is often completely covered in a process called Bagh. Phulkari is traditionally made from heavy fabrics like khaddar, but today it can be made from a variety of materials, including chiffon and lightweight cotton.

Traditionally worn by Punjabi women during festivals and weddings, Phulkari sarees are a symbol of joy and celebration. The 'phulkari' technique involves creating intricate designs on the back of the fabric, resulting in a beautiful mirrored effect on the front. Silken Thread offers a stunning collection of Phulkari pieces, each one a unique piece of cultural heritage.

A Textured Tale of Natural Beauty

Raw silk sarees, also known as 'Khadi silk,' celebrate the natural, unrefined texture of the silken threads. Unlike pure silk, which undergoes extensive processing to achieve a smooth finish, raw silk retains its slub and unevenness, creating a unique textural appeal. The weaving technique utilizes these coarse fibers, resulting in a fabric that is slightly heavier and sturdier than pure silk. Raw silk sarees are known for their earthy elegance and subtle sheen, making them a popular choice for those who appreciate a more organic and textured aesthetic.

title: Shibori
descriptionHtml:
Shibori is a manual tie-dyeing technique that creates uneven patterns on textiles. The word "shibori" comes from the Japanese word shiboru, which means "wring" or "squeeze. Shibori uses intricate stitches and combinations of stitches or dextrous ways of folding to achieve its effects, as against tie dye- which simply ties the fabric together using rubber bands or string.

Once dipped in vibrant colors, the fabric unveils stunning geometric or organic designs. Each Shibori fabric is one-of-a-kind, a testament to the artisan's skill and the inherent beauty of imperfections. Silkenthread has exclusive collection of shibori printed sarees in bhagalpuri silk, hand painted traditional kalamkari printed pallu.

title: Telia Rumal
descriptionHtml:
Telia Rumal sarees are a rare and exquisite textile tradition from Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, known for their intricate double ikat weaving technique. The name “Telia” comes from the practice of treating the yarn with castor ash and oil before dyeing, which not only enhances the colors but also gives the fabric a distinctive softness and sheen. Traditionally, these sarees were woven with geometric motifs, bold patterns, and deep hues of red, black, and white, each design carrying symbolic meaning. Their complex weaving process, which involves dyeing both warp and weft threads before weaving, makes every piece a true masterpiece of craftsmanship.

Historically, Telia Rumals were not just sarees but square cloths used as scarves, head coverings, or gifts, especially by traders and aristocrats. Over time, the craft evolved into sarees while still preserving the authenticity of its motifs, such as checks, diamonds, and temple-inspired designs. These sarees are considered auspicious and were often exchanged during important occasions. The richness of the craft reflects the skill of master weavers who guard the meticulous dyeing and weaving process, keeping alive a legacy passed down through generations.

Today, Telia Rumal sarees are treasured by connoisseurs of handloom textiles for their cultural depth and timeless appeal. They are celebrated not only for their visual beauty but also for the eco-friendly dyeing process and natural textures. As part of India’s precious ikat traditions, they hold a special place among collectors, heritage fashion lovers, and those who value sustainable craftsmanship. By wearing a Telia Rumal saree, one embraces not just a garment, but centuries of artistry, symbolism, and heritage woven into fabric.

title: Tussar silk
descriptionHtml:
Tussar silk, also known as Tussah or Kosa silk, is a coarse, copperish silk fabric made from the cocoons of silk moths. The silkworms feed on plants like asan and Arjun, lending it a distinct charm that sets it apart from cultivated silk varieties. Pure tussar silk sarees are hand spun and colored with natural dyes. The use of natural vegetable dyes makes the fabric eco-friendly and sustainable.

It is less lustrous than mulberry silk, but has its own unique feel and appeal. Tussar silk is mainly cultivated in India, particularly in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, and West Bengal. Bihar produces about 66% of Indian tussar, although much of it is woven in West Bengal and Orissa

Tussar silk is mainly used for furnishings and interiors. It has a coarse texture with a lustrous sheen giving it a very royal look
